title: CoMLRL Quick Start
content:
This tutorial demonstrates a simple two-agent training task with a length-ratio reward. Both agents receive the same prompt and generate independently; the second agent does not see the first agent’s response. The reward encourages the second output to contain 2–3× as many characters as the first. It does not evaluate story quality or semantic collaboration.
Run the example directly from an installed source checkout:
python examples/story-len-ratio.pyMemory requirements depend on the model, number of agents, batch size, and response length. W&B logging is disabled by default. To enable it, add --wandb (and optionally --wandb-project or --wandb-entity) to the command above.
Import Libraries# import math from functools import partial from datasets import Dataset from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer from comlrl.utils.reward_processor import RewardProcessors from comlrl.trainers.reinforce import MAGRPOConfig, MAGRPOTrainerDataset Preparation# We first create a dataset of creative prompts for the agents to work on.
train_data = { "prompt": [ "Describe a city in the clouds:", "Invent a new holiday and explain it:", "Write a bedtime story for a dragon:", "Explain how teleportation might work:", "Tell a joke about dinosaurs:", "Describe a world without electricity:", "Create a superhero with a unique power:", "Write a scene where the moon talks:", "Invent a new type of fruit:", "Design a playground on Mars:", ] } train_dataset = Dataset.from_dict(train_data)Agent Initialization# We load a tokenizer to convert text into tokens that the model can process and initialize two separate instances.
model_name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name) agents = [AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name) for _ in range(2)]Define the Reward Function# The reward function measures how well the agents collaborate. It gives maximum reward (1.0) when the second agent’s output is 2–3× longer than the first agent’s. If the length ratio falls outside this range, the reward decays exponentially based on how far it deviates.
def proper_length_ratio_reward( completions1, completions2, target_min=2.0, target_max=3.0 ): rewards = [] for c1, c2 in zip(completions1, completions2): len1, len2 = len(c1), len(c2) if len1 == 0: rewards.append(0.0) continue ratio = len2 / len1 if target_min <= ratio <= target_max: reward = 1.0 else: if ratio < target_min: distance = target_min - ratio else: distance = ratio - target_max reward = math.exp(-distance) rewards.append(float(reward)) return rewardsConfigure Training# We set up the training configuration with hyperparameters like learning rate, batch size, and the number of generations each agent produces per prompt.
output_dir = "./magrpo_multi_reward_output" config = MAGRPOConfig( num_train_epochs=3, agent_learning_rate=5e-5, logging_steps=10, num_generations=8, num_turns=1, max_new_tokens=128, )Create the Trainer# We instantiate the MAGRPO trainer with our agents, reward function, and configuration. RewardProcessors.scale multiplies task rewards by 100. With the default advantage_normalization=True, this positive scaling is largely canceled by normalization and should not be interpreted as a 100× stronger policy gradient.
configured_reward_func = partial( proper_length_ratio_reward, target_min=2, target_max=3 ) trainer = MAGRPOTrainer( agents=agents, reward_func=configured_reward_func, reward_processor=RewardProcessors.scale(factor=100.0), args=config, train_dataset=train_dataset, tokenizer=tokenizer, )Run Training# Finally, we start the training process. The trainer will optimize both agents to maximize the collaborative reward, then save the trained models.
trainer.train() trainer.save_model(f"{output_dir}/models")

title: Installation
content:
CoMLRL provides several different ways for installation. Python 3.10 or later is required. Install a PyTorch build compatible with your machine separately; it is intentionally excluded from the package’s core dependencies.
These docs describe the current source checkout. Published PyPI and conda-forge packages can lag behind it, so use the source installation for features added on the clean-up branch.
Install from PyPI# pip install comlrl # install PyTorch compatible with your deviceInstall from conda-forge# conda install -c conda-forge comlrl # install PyTorch compatible with your deviceInstall from source# To access the latest features of CoMLRL or to develop CoMLRL, clone this repository and install in editable mode:
git clone https://github.com/OpenMLRL/CoMLRL.git cd CoMLRL # To follow the version covered by these branch docs: git checkout clean-up pip install -e . # install PyTorch compatible with your device

title: Multi-Agent REINFORCE
content:
REINFORCE is a class of policy gradient methods that optimize the policy directly using sampled returns. It has been widely used to fine-tune LLMs because of its simplicity and efficiency, e.g., GRPO, Dr. GRPO, RLOO, ReMax, TreeRPO, and REINFORCE++. REINFORCE can be extended to multi-agent settings, where multiple LLM agents respond at each turn and their joint responses receive a shared reward.
MA-REINFORCE# The policy-gradient surrogate for Multi‑Agent REINFORCE (MA-REINFORCE), before advantage normalization or reference regularization, can be expressed as:
\[ J(\theta_i) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{o}_0 \sim \mathcal{D}, \mathbf{h}_t \sim \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} \Bigg[\sum_{t=0}^{H-1} R_t \cdot \log \pi_{\theta_i}(a_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})\Bigg], \] where \( R_t \) is the return at turn \( t \) and \( H \) is the horizon (i.e., number of dialog turns). The expectation is taken over initial observations from the dataset \( \mathcal{D} \) and the joint action history of all episodes following policy \( \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \).
REINFORCE methods do not use a critic model for value estimation. Their policy-gradient estimates can have high variance due to stochastic sampling and long-term credit assignment. Common ways to reduce this variance include using an action-independent baseline or averaging over more samples, e.g., \( K \) samples at each joint history \( \mathbf{h}_t \).
\[ J(\theta_i) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{o}_0 \sim \mathcal{D}, \mathbf{h}_t \sim \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} \Bigg[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \sum_{t=0}^{H-1} \left(R^{k}_t - b(\mathbf{h}_t)\right) \cdot \log \pi_{\theta_i}(a^{k}_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})\Bigg], \] where the baseline \( b(\mathbf{h}_t) \) is action-independent.
MAGRPO# Multi‑Agent Group‑Relative Policy Optimization (MAGRPO) is an instantiation of MA-REINFORCE inspired by GRPO, where the group-average baseline is the mean return of \( K \) samples. In the default aligned joint mode, its surrogate before advantage normalization is:
\[ J(\theta_i) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{o}_0 \sim \mathcal{D}, \mathbf{h}_t \sim \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} \Bigg[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1} \left(R^{k}_t - \frac{1}{K}\sum_{l=1}^{K}R^{l}_t\right) \cdot \log \pi_{\theta_i}(a^{k}_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})\Bigg]. \] The sampled group mean includes the sample being updated, so it is not the action-independent baseline assumed in the general expression above. In multi-turn training, each branch’s return is its immediate reward plus the mean return of its child node, with no discount applied. In cross mode, each agent’s completion instead receives the sum of returns over all joint combinations containing that completion.
By default, advantage_normalization=True then centers and scales the advantages within each node’s generation group using the population standard deviation, with a minimum denominator of 1e-6. If reference KL regularization is enabled, the sampled reference penalty is subtracted from returns before the baseline and normalization are applied.
The current MAGRPOTrainer loss slice omits the final completion token, so its implemented sequence score differs from the full sequence log-probability in the surrogate above. Use the canonical joint_mode="cross": the accepted "crossed" alias generates Cartesian combinations but does not apply the same per-completion return aggregation.
MAGRPOConfig Parameters num_agents: Configured number of agents; keep this consistent with the trainer setup num_turns: Number of turns per episode num_train_epochs: Number of training epochs agent_learning_rate: Learning rate logging_steps: Log every N steps num_generations: Number of generations to sample per prompt for each agent max_new_tokens: Maximum number of new tokens to generate temperature: Temperature for sampling top_p: Top-p for sampling top_k: Top-k for sampling discount: Retained configuration field; the current MAGRPO implementation computes undiscounted returns and does not use this value joint_mode: Joint action composition (aligned for index-aligned, cross for Cartesian product) early_termination_threshold: Stop expanding a training branch when its node’s mean immediate reward exceeds this threshold (default -0.2; None disables early termination) rollout_buffer_size: Number of node samples to buffer per agent before an update train_batch_size: Number of node samples per optimizer step; defaults to rollout_buffer_size advantage_normalization: Center and scale advantages within each node’s generation group (default True) eval_interval: Run evaluation at batch indices divisible by N, including the first batch of each epoch; 0 disables periodic evaluation eval_num_samples: Number of samples to evaluate per evaluation run eval_batch_size: Eval dataloader batch size external_prompt_passthrough: Use external prompts directly in multi-turn advantage_mode: Baseline mode (mean, max, rloo, raw) parallel_training: Agent execution mode (none or mp) agent_devices: Agent device placement; required explicitly for parallel_training="mp" reference_kl_enabled: Enable a frozen-reference KL penalty (default False) reference_kl_coef: Weight of the reference penalty (default 0.1) reference_devices: Optional device placement for the reference models MAGRPOTrainer Parameters agent_model or agents: Model identifier string for homogeneous agents, or a list of model identifiers or preloaded models; use agents for preloaded models num_agents: Number of agents created from agent_model (default 2); pass this explicitly even when it is set in args. When only agents is supplied, its length determines the agent count tokenizer: Shared tokenizer or one per agent; optional for model identifiers, required for preloaded models reward_func: Callable that returns a list of floats (required) reward_processor: Optional processor to apply to rewards (e.g., scaling) formatters: Single callable or list of callables for each agent to format prompts args: Instance of MAGRPOConfig (optional) train_dataset: Dataset required when calling train() eval_dataset: Evaluation dataset (optional) model_config: Model configuration dict (optional) wandb_config: Configuration for Weights & Biases logging (optional) external_transition: Function providing transitions between turns; required when num_turns > 1 (the default is 2) eval_logger: Optional task metrics, called as eval_logger(agent_completions_turns=..., batch_items=..., prompts=...); returns one metrics dict per evaluated item. Used together with eval_aggregator eval_aggregator: Optional, called as eval_aggregator(metrics, num_turns=...); the returned turn_k/... metrics are logged under eval/. Both evaluation callbacks must be supplied for custom metrics MAGRPO collects samples into a rollout buffer and recomputes their log probabilities during updates, without importance sampling or ratio clipping. Samples may therefore predate earlier updates from the same buffer or rollout tree. Since the trainer has no critic model, value_clip_range does not apply.
The trainer uses a fixed training DataLoader batch size of 1 and requires at least num_generations=2, including for the raw-return variant. By default, train_batch_size=rollout_buffer_size: each agent averages the losses of its buffered node samples for one optimizer step. Smaller mini-batches produce multiple optimizer steps; a partial buffer is flushed at the end of each epoch.
Other Variants# CoMLRL also provides other MA-REINFORCE variants with different baselines:
MARLOO: Multi‑Agent REINFORCE Leave‑One‑Out. The baseline is the mean return of the other generations in the same node’s sample group, not the other agents. \[ J(\theta_i) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{o}_0 \sim \mathcal{D}, \mathbf{h}_t \sim \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} \Bigg[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1} \left(R^{k}_t - \frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{l=1, l\neq k}^{K}R^{l}_t\right) \cdot \log \pi_{\theta_i}(a^{k}_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})\Bigg]. \] MAReMax: Multi‑Agent REINFORCE with Group Max (MAReMaxConfig and MAReMaxTrainer). The baseline is the maximum sampled group return at the node; this implementation does not generate a separate greedy baseline response. \[ J(\theta_i) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{o}_0 \sim \mathcal{D}, \mathbf{h}_t \sim \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} \Bigg[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1} \left(R^{k}_t - \mathrm{max}_l\, R^l_t \right) \cdot \log \pi_{\theta_i}(a^{k}_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})\Bigg]. \] MAREINFORCETrainer, MARLOOTrainer, and MAReMaxTrainer derive from comlrl.trainers.reinforce.MAGRPOTrainer. Their corresponding configuration classes inherit MAGRPOConfig, with default advantage_mode values of raw, rloo, and max respectively. They share the same trainer interface and configuration fields.
The variant formulas describe advantages before normalization. All variants inherit advantage_normalization=True, which re-centers even raw returns and max-baseline advantages. Except for the standard-deviation floor and numerical precision, the four modes then yield the same normalized advantages. Set advantage_normalization=False to retain the baseline differences shown above, including the raw-return MA-REINFORCE estimator.

title: Training Paradigms
content:
An actor generates the responses being learned; an iterative comparator supplies alternative responses to the same task. Choose their generation layouts separately from the comparator’s policy source. Both layouts can be used with the MADPO and MARLHF objectives.
Collaboration Modes# collaboration_mode determines the trainable actor layout. comparator_generation_mode determines the comparator layout in iterative training.
Actor layout Comparator layout Joint responses Decentralized Decentralized Each role generates its own response on both sides of the comparison. Decentralized Centralized Separate actors are compared with one comparator that writes all roles’ responses. Centralized Centralized One actor and one comparator each write a complete joint response. In decentralized mode, each agent has its own policy and generates its own response. MADPO combines their preference margins, while MARLHF learns one reward from the joint responses.
In centralized mode, one actor receives every role’s prompt and generates one complete joint response. Keep num_agents equal to the number of task roles, but pass exactly one actor and tokenizer. Training and learned reward scoring retain the joint text; role parsing happens at task reward and evaluation boundaries. max_new_tokens is the total joint-response budget.
All four preference trainers currently require num_turns=1 and joint_mode="aligned". Centralized actor training forces centralized comparator generation in the iterative configurations; a centralized actor with a decentralized comparator is not a separate supported layout.
Centralized Preference Collaboration# MADPOConfig, MARLHFConfig, and their iterative variants accept collaboration_mode="centralized" (default: "decentralized"). In this mode, one trainable actor receives all role prompts and generates one joint response. The complete response, including role delimiters, is optimized by one actor and one optimizer. Later roles are causally conditioned on earlier roles.
The default TaggedCentralizedComparatorAdapter uses indexed role tags. To customize the joint prompt and response format, pass a downstream centralized_comparator_adapter implementing build_prompt and parse_completion. The same adapter is used for the actor and comparator; domain instructions and parsing stay outside CoMLRL. Parsing happens only at the task reward and evaluation boundaries. Preference replay, learned reward scoring, and policy training keep the complete joint text.
Keep num_agents equal to the number of task roles (for example, 2). Use agent_model once, or supply exactly one entry in agents and its tokenizer. agent_devices describes one actor. The optional reward model and external comparator retain their independent device settings. Centralized actor training currently requires num_turns=1. If reference KL is enabled, reference_devices also describes one actor. MADPO retains its existing reference-free preference objective; MARLHF’s online RL phase uses the configured KL penalty. Iterative trainers force comparator_generation_mode="centralized" and require comparator_centralized_agent_index=0. Current, current-copy, history, model, and API comparator sources retain their existing meanings. max_new_tokens is the total joint response budget, not a per-role budget. Consider doubling a previous per-role limit. For MARLHF, also allow enough reward_max_length for the joint prompt and both outputs. One joint completion still counts as one environment step; a preference pair uses environment_steps_per_pair (default 2). Role count does not multiply these counters. Checkpoints contain one actor (agent_0). W&B records collaboration_mode, num_roles, num_actor_models, and the effective comparator generation mode. Decentralized collaboration continues to use the existing separate-actor generation, loss, and evaluation paths.
Comparator Generation# For decentralized actors, select either comparator_generation_mode="decentralized" (the default) or "centralized". A decentralized comparator generates one response per role. A centralized comparator receives the combined prompt and generates all role responses together.
The default TaggedCentralizedComparatorAdapter uses indexed <agent_0>...</agent_0> sections. A custom centralized_comparator_adapter defines the joint prompt through build_prompt and returns exactly one string per role through parse_completion.
When the actors are decentralized, the centralized comparator’s joint text is parsed into role responses before constructing preference pairs. When the actor is also centralized, the joint text is retained throughout preference learning and is parsed only for task reward and evaluation.
Comparator generation parameters:
comparator_generation_mode: Separate role responses ("decentralized") or one joint response ("centralized") comparator_centralized_agent_index: Actor or checkpoint role index used for centralized comparator generation with current, current-copy, or history policies; defaults to 0. It must be within the configured role range, and centralized actor training requires 0 centralized_comparator_adapter: Trainer argument supplying the shared joint prompt builder and role parser The comparator’s model source, candidate count, and devices are documented in Comparator.
Iterative Training# MADPOIterTrainer and MARLHFIterTrainer alternate preference collection with training. Each collection round compares a new sample from the current policy with a sample from a comparator policy at the same candidate index. Either policy can supply the winner; reward ties are skipped.
MADPOIter refreshes the pairs and runs MADPO updates for num_train_epochs per iteration. MARLHFIter refreshes the pairs, initializes and trains a reward model, and runs the selected online RL algorithm for each iteration. Import the iterative configurations and trainers from comlrl.trainers.preference.
MADPOIterConfig Parameters Inherits MADPOConfig; num_train_epochs applies to each iteration num_iterations: Number of preference-refresh and training rounds pair_selection: Adds "comparator_reward" (the iterative default), which prioritizes higher comparator rewards, then larger reward gaps Comparator source and generation settings: see Comparator and Comparator Generation Replay selection, sample size, and storage settings: see Replay Buffer The iterative pair_selection="all" retains all non-tied index-aligned current-versus-comparator comparisons, with preference_pairs_per_sample=None. An iteration refreshes preference data and then trains on the selected replay pairs; it is not a dialog turn.
MARLHFIterConfig Parameters Combines the MARLHF settings with the iterative comparator and replay settings above preference_scoring_reward: "task" (default) labels new comparisons with the task reward; "reward_model" uses the previous iteration’s learned reward model once one is available, starting with task rewards in the first iteration reward_num_train_epochs: Reward-model training epochs per iteration

title: Comparator
content:
A comparator supplies candidate responses for MADPOIterTrainer and MARLHFIterTrainer. The trainer compares current-policy and comparator responses at the same candidate index. Either side can win; tied rewards do not form a preference pair.
Choose the source with comparator_policy. Choose whether it generates separate role responses or one joint response in Training Paradigms.
Policy Sources# Policy Response source current Active actor weights, sampled with a separate comparator random-number stream. current_copy Current actor weights, with optional placement on separate comparator devices. model Explicit model identifiers or model sources supplied for the comparator. history A saved earlier actor checkpoint. api A remote model endpoint. current is the default. current_copy uses the same policy weights; when comparator and actor devices match, it reuses the actor models. With separate devices, the comparator copies are prepared for that iteration’s collection phase and released afterward.
For history, comparator_history_k=1 selects the preceding iteration’s saved policy. Before a sufficiently old checkpoint exists, the trainer falls back to the initial policy. Policy checkpoints are saved automatically for this comparator mode.
Comparator parameters:
comparator_policy: "current", "current_copy", "model", "history", or "api" comparator_num_candidates: Comparator sample count; defaults to preference_num_candidates comparator_model_name or comparator_agents: Required model source(s) for comparator_policy="model" comparator_history_k: How many iterations back to select a policy checkpoint; defaults to 1 for "history" comparator_devices: Device placement for local comparator models policy_checkpoint_dir: Optional actor-checkpoint output location; specifying it also enables checkpoint saving for other comparator modes The current-policy and comparator sample counts can differ, but comparisons only use candidate indices available on both sides. pair_selection="comparator_reward" prioritizes comparisons with higher comparator rewards and then larger reward gaps. It does not assume that the comparator is always the preferred response.
Local Models# Use comparator_model_name for a shared model source, or comparator_agents for explicit sources. A decentralized comparator uses one model per actor. A centralized comparator uses one model selected for the joint prompt; comparator_agents may contain one source or one source per actor, in which case comparator_centralized_agent_index selects the source.
Model identifiers can point to a compatible model repository or a local checkpoint. The common model-loading settings are described in Model Loading.
Example local comparator overrides:
comparator_policy=model comparator_model_name=/path/to/comparator-checkpoint comparator_generation_mode=centralized comparator_centralized_agent_index=0 comparator_devices=cuda:1API Comparators# Iterative MADPO and MARLHF can use a remote model with comparator_policy=api. The existing comparator_api_format=openai path remains compatible with OpenAI-style Chat Completions endpoints such as DeepSeek. Two native formats are also supported:
anthropic: Anthropic Messages API. Use https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and a model such as claude-sonnet-4-20250514. openai_responses (or responses/codex): OpenAI Responses API. Use https://api.openai.com/v1/responses, OPENAI_API_KEY, and a model such as gpt-5.1-codex. The native APIs are queried once per candidate because they do not use the Chat Completions n parameter. The prompt remains the same centralized or decentralized comparator prompt, and the trainer extracts text from the provider-specific response format.
Example Anthropic comparator overrides:
comparator_policy=api comparator_api_format=anthropic comparator_api_url=https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages comparator_api_model=claude-sonnet-4-20250514 comparator_api_key_env=ANTHROPIC_API_KEYExample OpenAI/Codex comparator overrides:
comparator_policy=api comparator_api_format=openai_responses comparator_api_url=https://api.openai.com/v1/responses comparator_api_model=gpt-5.1-codex comparator_api_key_env=OPENAI_API_KEYAPI Parameters# Comparator API parameters:
comparator_api_url: Required endpoint URL when comparator_policy="api" comparator_api_format: "generic" (default), "openai" for Chat Completions, "anthropic" for Messages, or "openai_responses" for Responses comparator_api_model: Model name passed to the remote endpoint comparator_api_key_env: Environment variable from which to read the API key comparator_api_key: Optional explicitly supplied key comparator_api_headers: Additional request headers comparator_api_key_header, comparator_api_key_prefix: Authentication header and prefix; defaults are "Authorization" and "Bearer", with native Anthropic header handling comparator_api_timeout: Request timeout in seconds; defaults to 120 comparator_api_max_n_per_request: Maximum candidates requested in each Chat Completions call; useful for endpoints that limit n comparator_api_response_field: Field used for completions in a generic response; defaults to "completions" comparator_api_extra_body: Additional request-body fields For the generic format, the request includes the prompt, actor index, task item, candidate count, and generation settings. The response parser reads comparator_api_response_field. Native formats use their provider-specific payload and text extraction.

title: MARL
content: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning trains collaborating policies from task rewards. Explore Multi-Agent REINFORCE for critic-free updates, or Multi-Agent Actor-Critic for value-based training.

title: Model Loading & Saving
content:
CoMLRL supports both homogeneous and heterogeneous models. Users can assign agent_model/critic_model with HuggingFace model identifiers for homogeneous setups, or provide agents/critics lists for heterogeneous setups.
Local model directories are also supported. You can save trained actors, load their weights into a new trainer, and train them further. The sections below cover model loading, the saved directory layout, and which training state must be initialized again.
The examples below assume you have defined a task-specific reward_func and train_dataset, as shown in the quick start. They use num_turns=1; multi-turn training additionally requires an external_transition.
from transformers import AutoTokenizer from comlrl.trainers.reinforce import MAGRPOConfig, MAGRPOTrainer from comlrl.trainers.actor_critic import IACConfig, IACTrainer, MAACConfig, MAACTrainerHomogeneous Agents# The easiest way to start the journey of CoMLRL is to load num_agents homogeneous agents with a single model identifier. Set agent_model to a model identifier string while keeping agents=None. For MAGRPO, pass the actor count directly as the trainer’s num_agents argument; setting only MAGRPOConfig.num_agents does not change the number of homogeneous actors.
For example, to load 3 Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B agents:
trainer = MAGRPOTrainer( agent_model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B", agents=None, num_agents=3, reward_func=reward_func, train_dataset=train_dataset, args=MAGRPOConfig(num_agents=3, num_turns=1, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, top_k=None), )Heterogeneous Agents# Although homogeneous LLM agents can be specified into different roles by prompting, using heterogeneous LLMs with different skills can further unleash the potential of multi-agent collaboration. Pass model identifier strings or loaded model objects in agents, and pass compatible tokenizers separately through tokenizer. MAGRPO infers the actor count from agents when agent_model=None; MAAC/IAC require the list length to match args.num_agents. For MAGRPO, use a list of identifiers or a list of loaded objects, without mixing the two. When agents is provided, set agent_model=None. If both are provided, they must match (same model names and correct length), otherwise training raises an error.
For example, to load a Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-3B and a Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B:
trainer = MAGRPOTrainer( agent_model=None, agents=["Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-3B", "Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B"], reward_func=reward_func, train_dataset=train_dataset, args=MAGRPOConfig(num_agents=2, num_turns=1, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, top_k=None), )Loading LLM Critics# The loading of critics depends on the algorithm and the use_separate_critic setting. In Multi-Agent Actor-Critic (MAAC), one separate centralized critic is provided through critic_model or a one-element critics list. It must be a supported causal language model: the trainer adds a value head and encodes the joint input with the first actor’s tokenizer, so that tokenizer must also be compatible with the critic.
For example, to load a Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-3B and a Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B with a centralized Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B critic:
trainer = MAACTrainer( agent_model=None, agents=["Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-3B", "Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B"], tokenizer=[ AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-3B"), AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B"), ], critic_model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B", critics=None, reward_func=reward_func, train_dataset=train_dataset, args=MAACConfig(num_agents=2, num_turns=1, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, top_k=None), )In Independent Actor-Critic (IAC), each agent can have its own critic. When use_separate_critic=True, provide one critic_model identifier to load a separate copy per agent, or a critics list of length num_agents. Each separate critic receives token IDs from its corresponding actor’s tokenizer and must be compatible with it. When use_separate_critic=false, each agent shares its LLM agent backbone with its critic, and the critic is loaded at the same time as the agent. In this case, critic_model and critics should not be provided and set to null or None. Similarly to agents, if both critic_model and critics are provided, they must match (same names, correct length) or training will raise an error.
For example, to load a Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-3B and a Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with separate critics of the same models:
trainer = IACTrainer( agent_model=None, agents=["Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-3B", "Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B"], tokenizer=[ AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-3B"), AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B"), ], critic_model=None, critics=["Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-3B", "Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B"], reward_func=reward_func, train_dataset=train_dataset, args=IACConfig( num_agents=2, num_turns=1, use_separate_critic=True, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, top_k=None, ), )Or actor can share the same model with its critic:
trainer = IACTrainer( agent_model=None, agents=["Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-3B", "Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B"], tokenizer=[ AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-3B"), AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B"), ], critic_model=None, critics=None, reward_func=reward_func, train_dataset=train_dataset, args=IACConfig( num_agents=2, num_turns=1, use_separate_critic=False, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, top_k=None, ), ) Internally, trainers always work with agents/critics lists. agent_model and critic_model are convenience shortcuts for homogeneous settings; if both are provided, they must be consistent.
MAGRPO loads tokenizers automatically for model identifier strings. MAAC/IAC load a tokenizer automatically for agent_model, but require an explicit tokenizer when agents is supplied, even if it contains strings. For loaded model objects, provide one compatible shared tokenizer or a tokenizer list matching the actors. Heterogeneous actors may have different vocabularies when each uses its own compatible tokenizer; separate critics must also accept their actor’s token IDs (the first actor’s IDs for MAAC).
Saving Models# Call save_model(output_dir) explicitly after training. It writes the actors’ Hugging Face model configuration, weights, and tokenizers to local directories:
trainer.train() trainer.save_model("./saved-models/run-1")The directory layout depends on the trainer. In the table, output_dir is the directory passed to save_model, and i is the zero-based actor index.
Trainer Actor and tokenizer Additional saved weights MA-REINFORCE family, including MAGRPO output_dir/agent_i/ None MADPO, MARLHF, and their iterative variants output_dir/agent_i/ None IAC, one actor output_dir/ Shared head: value_head.pt; separate critic: critic/ with its own value_head.pt IAC, multiple actors output_dir/agent_i/ Shared head: agent_i/value_head.pt; separate critic: agent_i/critic/ with its own value_head.pt MAAC output_dir/agent_i/ One centralized critic in output_dir/critic/, including value_head.pt Paths without an output_dir prefix are relative to output_dir. Critic directories contain the critic backbone configuration and weights; they use the corresponding actor’s tokenizer, or the first actor’s tokenizer for MAAC.
The MA-REINFORCE and preference trainers use agent_0/ even with one actor. Centralized MAPL also saves one actor in agent_0/, while num_agents continues to describe the number of task roles.
MARLHF’s inherited save_model exports the actors and tokenizers. It does not export the learned reward model, reward head, or critics created by its online actor-critic backend.
Training from Saved Models# To continue training a saved two-actor MAGRPO setup, pass each actor’s directory in the original role order. The parent run-1 directory is a container for the actors; each agent_i directory is a loadable model.
from comlrl.trainers.reinforce import MAGRPOConfig, MAGRPOTrainer continued_trainer = MAGRPOTrainer( agents=[ "./saved-models/run-1/agent_0", "./saved-models/run-1/agent_1", ], num_agents=2, reward_func=reward_func, train_dataset=train_dataset, args=MAGRPOConfig( num_agents=2, num_turns=1, num_train_epochs=3, agent_learning_rate=5e-6, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, top_k=None, ), ) continued_trainer.train() continued_trainer.save_model("./saved-models/run-2")MAGRPO loads the tokenizers from those actor directories automatically. Here, num_train_epochs=3 means three epochs in the new training run. Supply the dataset, reward function, training configuration, and any custom formatters, reward processor, or external transition again; these are not stored by save_model.
Use the same local-directory approach with the other trainers, retaining their tokenizer and actor-count requirements described above. For centralized MAPL, provide only the saved agent_0 model, retain the original task-role count, and set collaboration_mode="centralized" again. Preference trainers start their preference collection and reward-learning stages according to the new run’s configuration.
Restoring Value Heads# IAC and MAAC save value heads separately as value_head.pt. Loading a critic or shared actor directory through the constructor restores the language-model backbone and creates a new value head. Load the saved head explicitly before calling train() to retain its learned values.
For a saved two-actor MAAC setup using the default linear value head:
from pathlib import Path import torch from transformers import AutoTokenizer from comlrl.trainers.actor_critic import MAACConfig, MAACTrainer saved_dir = Path("./saved-models/maac-run-1") actor_dirs = [str(saved_dir / f"agent_{i}") for i in range(2)] continued_maac = MAACTrainer( agents=actor_dirs, tokenizer=[AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(path) for path in actor_dirs], critic_model=str(saved_dir / "critic"), reward_func=reward_func, train_dataset=train_dataset, args=MAACConfig(num_agents=2, num_turns=1, num_train_epochs=3), ) continued_maac.critics[0].value_head.load_state_dict( torch.load( saved_dir / "critic" / "value_head.pt", map_location="cpu", weights_only=True, ) ) continued_maac.train() continued_maac.save_model("./saved-models/maac-run-2")For IAC, use the same load_state_dict step on continued_iac.agents[i].value_head when use_separate_critic=False, or on continued_iac.critics[i].value_head when it is True. Load each head from the corresponding path in the saving table; load separate critic backbones through critic_model or critics as well.
The value-head architecture must match the saved run. For IAC, reuse IACConfig.value_head_hidden_dim for shared heads and IACConfig.critic_value_head_hidden_dim for separate heads. For a custom MAAC head, pass the original model_config={"critic_value_head_hidden_dim": ...} when constructing the trainer. Keep the original critic_type ("v" or "q") when continuing the same value-learning setup.
Training State# Saved weights support further training, but CoMLRL currently has no complete resume_from_checkpoint implementation. save_model does not save or restore optimizer state, scheduler state, epoch or environment-step counters, random-number-generator state, or rollout buffers. A new trainer creates fresh optimizers and starts its counters again.
When reference KL is enabled, a new trainer builds its frozen reference models from the actor sources supplied to that constructor. Reloading trained actors therefore uses those reloaded weights as the new reference, rather than restoring the previous run’s reference models.
Iterative MAPL’s policy_checkpoint_dir stores actor snapshots for comparator history. Its persisted preference pairs and replay files are also separate from save_model; creating a new iterative trainer does not automatically reconstruct the previous iteration or replay state from those files. See Comparator and Replay Buffer for their roles in an active run.

title: Multi-Agent Actor-Critic
content:
Actor-Critic (AC) methods are widely-used policy gradient methods that employ critics to facilitate training. AC methods can achieve lower variance and better sample efficiency than REINFORCE, but this requires careful design and tuning of the critic to ensure stable training. In Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), Actor-Critic methods can be instantiated as Multi-Agent Actor-Critic (MAAC) and Independent Actor-Critic (IAC).
MAAC# Multi-Agent Actor-Critic (MAAC) uses one Centralized Critic (CC) across agents to evaluate joint histories with critic_type="v", or joint history-action pairs with critic_type="q". The critic receives the agents’ prompts joined into one text; Q mode also includes their generated completions.
Write the critic prediction as \( C_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(x_t) \), where \( x_t=\mathbf{h}_t \) in V mode and \( x_t=(\mathbf{h}_t,\mathbf{a}_t) \) in Q mode. CoMLRL forms a one-step target and a TD residual for each agent:
\[ y_{i,t}=\tilde r_{i,t}+\gamma m_t\bar C(x_{t+1}), \qquad A_{i,t}=y_{i,t}-\bar C(x_t), \] where \( \bar C \) is the detached prediction recorded during rollout collection, and \( m_t \) is 1 only when another turn was collected. The final collected turn, including an early-terminated or single-turn rollout, uses \( y_{i,t}=\tilde r_{i,t} \) without bootstrapping. Rewards may be shared across agents or supplied per agent. Here \( \tilde r_{i,t} \) denotes the processed reward, with the optional reference-KL penalty subtracted when enabled.
The actor and critic minimize the following losses over each agent’s mini-batch \( B_i \):
\[ \mathcal L_{\pi_i}=-\frac{1}{|B_i|}\sum_{t\in B_i}\log\pi_{\theta_i}(a_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})\,\operatorname{sg}(\widehat A_{i,t}), \qquad \mathcal L_C=\frac{1}{|B_i|}\sum_{t\in B_i}\big(C_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(x_t)-y_{i,t}\big)^2. \] Here \( \widehat A \) is the optionally normalized residual and \( \operatorname{sg} \) means stop-gradient. The completion log-probability is the sum of generated-token log-probabilities; prompt and trailing padding tokens are excluded. The loss then averages across samples. Buffers are grouped by agent and turn before updating, and advantage_normalization normalizes the residuals within each such group. Targets and advantages remain fixed during the update. The shared critic is updated sequentially with each agent’s batch, and value_loss_coef scales its loss.
In Q mode, the implementation uses the same TD-residual actor weight, with a sampled next action in the bootstrap. It does not implement a separate actor objective weighted directly by Q or a state-only baseline for Q.
MAACConfig Parameters num_agents: Number of agents num_turns: Number of turns critic_type: Critic target type (v for V(h), q for Q(h,a)) num_train_epochs: Number of training epochs agent_learning_rate: Learning rate for agents critic_learning_rate: Learning rate for shared critic value_loss_coef: Weight on critic loss advantage_normalization: Whether to normalize advantages before updates rollout_buffer_size: Number of samples to collect per agent before an update train_batch_size: Mini-batch size within each update max_new_tokens: Maximum tokens to generate per completion temperature: Temperature for sampling top_p: Top-p for nucleus sampling top_k: Top-k for sampling num_generations: Number of generations per prompt per agent external_prompt_passthrough: Use external prompts directly in multi-turn discount: Discount factor for the next-turn critic prediction in TD targets; logged expected_return uses undiscounted reward sums early_termination_threshold: Stop after a turn when its mean processed reward exceeds this threshold; None disables early stopping eval_interval: Evaluation interval (in training batches) eval_num_samples: Number of evaluation samples per interval eval_batch_size: Eval dataloader batch size logging_steps: Minimum number of joint-action reward evaluations between training metric logs parallel_training: none for one device or mp for explicit agent/critic device placement agent_devices, critic_devices: Device assignments, required in mp mode reference_kl_enabled, reference_kl_coef: Enable and weight the frozen-reference KL reward penalty (disabled by default) reference_devices: Optional device placement for reference models MAACTrainer Parameters agent_model or agents: Actor model identifier string for homogeneous agents, or list of agent models (multi-agent agent_model must be a string) critic_model or critics: Required single shared critic, supplied as an identifier, model instance, or 1-element list tokenizer: Shared tokenizer, or a per-agent list when using agents; required with agents or a model instance, otherwise loaded from agent_model reward_func: Callable returning rewards (required) reward_processor: Optional reward post-processor formatters: Single callable or list for per-agent prompt formatting args: Instance of MAACConfig (optional) train_dataset: Training dataset (required) eval_dataset: Optional evaluation dataset model_config: Model loading options; critic_value_head_hidden_dim configures the centralized critic’s value head (optional) wandb_config: Weights & Biases logging config (optional) metrics_callback: Optional callback taking rollout samples and returning a dictionary of scalar metrics external_transition: Transition function required when num_turns > 1 MAAC updates on collected samples without importance sampling or policy-ratio clipping. MAACConfig has no value_clip_range option. The shared critic uses the first agent’s tokenizer, which must be compatible with the critic model.
The trainer uses a fixed training DataLoader batch size of 1. For num_turns > 1, provide an external_transition and set num_generations=1. train_batch_size defaults to rollout_buffer_size; actual updates use the available samples in each agent/turn group, including smaller groups when buffers are flushed.
IAC# Independent Actor-Critic (IAC) optimizes each agent’s policy with its own critic; other agents serve as part of the environment. Rewards can be shared or agent-specific. The critic conditions on that agent’s prompt/history in V mode, or its prompt and completion in Q mode. Using the same detached-target convention as MAAC:
\[ y_{i,t}=\tilde r_{i,t}+\gamma m_t\bar C_i(x_{i,t+1}), \qquad A_{i,t}=y_{i,t}-\bar C_i(x_{i,t}), \] where \( x_{i,t}=h_{i,t} \) in V mode and \( x_{i,t}=(h_{i,t},a_{i,t}) \) in Q mode. The actor uses the same sample-averaged loss and completion-token sum as MAAC, with optional normalization within each agent/turn group. The Q-mode actor also uses this TD residual.
CoMLRL supports two IAC variants:
Separate Critic: Uses an independent model for value estimation. Actor and critic parameters are optimized separately, at the cost of storing an additional model per agent.
Shared Model: Attaches a small value-head to the transformer backbone, sharing the actor model’s history (or history-action) representations to reduce the space costs.
The critics are updated by minimizing the TD error:
\[ \mathcal L_{C_i}=\frac{1}{|B_i|}\sum_{t\in B_i}\big(C_{\phi_i}(x_{i,t})-y_{i,t}\big)^2. \] When using a shared model (use_separate_critic=False), the actor and value head optimize the combined loss \( \mathcal L_{\pi_i}+\texttt{value\_loss\_coef}\,\mathcal L_{C_i} \). Unless value_clip_range=None, the value loss takes the larger error from the current prediction and a prediction clipped relative to the rollout value, for either critic type:
\[ \ell_{C_i}=\max\Big((C_{\phi_i}(x_{i,t})-y_{i,t})^2,\ (C_{\phi_i}^{\mathrm{clip}}(x_{i,t})-y_{i,t})^2\Big), \\ C_{\phi_i}^{\mathrm{clip}}(x)=\bar C_i(x)+\operatorname{clip}\big(C_{\phi_i}(x)-\bar C_i(x),-\epsilon,\epsilon\big), \] where \( \epsilon \) is value_clip_range and these errors are averaged across the mini-batch. Separate critics use the unclipped squared error.
IACConfig Parameters num_agents: Number of agents num_turns: Number of turns num_train_epochs: Number of training epochs agent_learning_rate: Learning rate for agents critic_learning_rate: Learning rate for separate critics; shared models use agent_learning_rate for both actor and value head value_loss_coef: Coefficient for value loss value_clip_range: Value clipping range in shared-model mode; None disables clipping advantage_normalization: Whether to normalize advantages rollout_buffer_size: Number of samples to collect before update train_batch_size: Mini-batch size for policy updates max_new_tokens: Maximum new tokens to generate temperature: Temperature for sampling top_p: Top-p for nucleus sampling top_k: Top-k for sampling num_generations: Number of generations per prompt per agent use_separate_critic: Whether to use separate critic model critic_type: Critic target type (v for V(h), q for Q(h,a)) critic_value_head_hidden_dim: Hidden dimension for critic value head value_head_hidden_dim: Hidden dimension for value head in shared-critic mode external_prompt_passthrough: Use external prompts directly in multi-turn discount: Discount factor in TD targets; logged expected_return uses undiscounted reward sums early_termination_threshold: Stop when a turn’s mean processed reward exceeds this threshold; None disables early stopping eval_interval: Evaluation interval (in training batches) eval_num_samples: Number of evaluation samples per interval eval_batch_size: Eval dataloader batch size logging_steps: Minimum number of joint-action reward evaluations between training metric logs parallel_training: none for one device or mp for explicit agent/critic device placement agent_devices, critic_devices: Device assignments; mp requires agent_devices and, for separate critics, critic_devices reference_kl_enabled, reference_kl_coef: Enable and weight the frozen-reference KL reward penalty (disabled by default) reference_devices: Optional device placement for reference models IACTrainer Parameters agent_model or agents: Model identifier string for homogeneous agents, or list of agent models (multi-agent agent_model must be a string) critic_model or critics: Critic identifier, model instance, or list of critic models when use_separate_critic=True tokenizer: Shared tokenizer, or a per-agent list when using agents; required with agents or a model instance, otherwise loaded from agent_model reward_func: Callable that returns a list of floats (required) reward_processor: Optional processor to apply to rewards formatters: Single callable or list of callables for each agent to format dataset items into prompts args: Instance of IACConfig (optional) train_dataset: Training dataset (required) eval_dataset: Evaluation dataset (optional) model_config: Model configuration dict (optional) wandb_config: Configuration for Weights & Biases logging (optional) metrics_callback: Optional callback taking rollout samples and returning a dictionary of scalar metrics external_transition: Optional transition function required for multi-turn training IAC updates on collected samples without importance sampling or policy-ratio clipping. In shared-model mode (use_separate_critic=False), value heads are attached to the actor models; passing critic_model or critics raises an error, and value_clip_range only applies in this mode. Agents may be homogeneous or heterogeneous. In separate-critic mode (use_separate_critic=True), pass a critics list of length num_agents or a single critic_model source to be broadcast. Use distinct model instances or an identifier that is loaded separately for each critic to keep their parameters independent; broadcasting one preloaded model object reuses its parameters. Each critic consumes its actor’s token IDs, so a different critic model must be compatible with that actor’s tokenizer.
The trainer uses a fixed training DataLoader batch size of 1. For num_turns > 1, provide an external_transition and set num_generations=1. train_batch_size defaults to rollout_buffer_size; actual updates use the available samples in each agent/turn group, including smaller groups when buffers are flushed.

title: Dataset Loading
content:
Keep task inputs and metadata together in a dataset and reserve a separate evaluation split. This guide uses the length-ratio task from the quick start to prepare data for training and evaluation.
Dataset Splits# Each dataset row is a dictionary. The default formatter reads its prompt field; additional fields can hold targets, labels, test cases, or other information needed by your reward function. Trainers pass the original row to the reward function through batch_items.
from datasets import Dataset dataset = Dataset.from_dict({ "prompt": [ "Describe a city in the clouds.", "Invent a new holiday.", "Write a bedtime story for a dragon.", "Explain how teleportation might work.", "Tell a story about dinosaurs.", "Describe a world without electricity.", "Create a superhero with a unique power.", "Write a scene where the moon talks.", "Invent a new type of fruit.", "Design a playground on Mars.", ], "target_min": [2.0] * 10, "target_max": [3.0] * 10, }) split = dataset.train_test_split(test_size=0.2, seed=42) train_dataset = split["train"] eval_dataset = split["test"]Here, eight rows are used for training and two are held out for evaluation. seed makes the split repeatable; it does not set the random seed for model generation. If your dataset already provides separate training and validation splits, pass those directly instead.
The current training data loaders preserve dataset order. Use train_dataset.shuffle(seed=42) before creating the trainer if you want a shuffled order; this produces a fixed order rather than a new shuffle each epoch.
Prompts and Rewards# Pass one formatter to share a prompt format across agents, or a list of formatters in actor order to assign different roles. Only fields used by the formatter enter the model prompt; the reward function can still read the full row.
import math def brief_formatter(item): return f"Write a short response to this task:\n{item['prompt']}" def detailed_formatter(item): return f"Write a detailed response to this task:\n{item['prompt']}" formatters = [brief_formatter, detailed_formatter] def reward_func(brief_completions, detailed_completions, *, batch_items): item = batch_items[0] rewards = [] for brief, detailed in zip(brief_completions, detailed_completions): if not brief: rewards.append(0.0) continue ratio = len(detailed) / len(brief) distance = max(item["target_min"] - ratio, ratio - item["target_max"], 0.0) rewards.append(math.exp(-distance)) return rewardsEach completion argument is a list of strings for one agent. The trainers used here call the reward function for one dataset row at a time, with that row available as batch_items[0]. This function returns one shared reward per aligned pair of responses. The task rewards a character-count ratio; it does not measure writing quality, and the agents generate independently.
You can check the data and reward without loading any models:
item = train_dataset[0] assert item["prompt"] in brief_formatter(item) assert reward_func(["Hi"], ["Hello"], batch_items=[item]) == [1.0] assert reward_func([""], ["Hello"], batch_items=[item]) == [0.0]For multi-turn tasks, formatters may also accept external_prompts. See Multi-Turn Interaction for the transition interface.
Training and Evaluation# Supply train_dataset and eval_dataset separately. Evaluation uses the same formatters and reward function as training, without updating model weights. It still samples model outputs using the generation settings, so repeated evaluations can produce different scores.
from comlrl.trainers.reinforce import MAGRPOConfig, MAGRPOTrainer config = MAGRPOConfig( num_agents=2, num_turns=1, num_train_epochs=1, num_generations=4, max_new_tokens=128, eval_interval=4, eval_num_samples=len(eval_dataset), eval_batch_size=1, logging_steps=4, ) trainer = MAGRPOTrainer( agent_model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B", num_agents=2, formatters=formatters, reward_func=reward_func, train_dataset=train_dataset, eval_dataset=eval_dataset, args=config, ) trainer.train() metrics = trainer.evaluate(num_eval_samples=len(eval_dataset)) print(metrics)For the MA-REINFORCE family, IAC, and MAAC, eval_interval counts training dataset items: evaluation runs before item zero of each epoch, then every configured interval. Set it to 0 for manual evaluation only. eval_num_samples limits the number of dataset rows evaluated, starting from the beginning of the evaluation split. Use a positive count; to evaluate the entire split, use its length. eval_batch_size controls the evaluation data loader batch size, not the number of generated responses per agent.
MAGRPO, IAC, and MAAC generate one response per agent per turn during evaluation. IAC and MAAC use their rollout collection path, with the configured turn structure, but their evaluate() method takes no sample-count argument:
# For an existing IACTrainer or MAACTrainer: ac_trainer.args.eval_num_samples = len(eval_dataset) metrics = ac_trainer.evaluate()Without an eval_dataset, evaluate() returns an empty dictionary. For MAPL, manual evaluate(num_eval_samples=...) is also available; the automatic evaluation schedule follows the preference-update or actor-training stage rather than the dataset-item schedule above.
See Logging Metric for saving evaluation results, recording training curves, and adding custom metrics.

title: MAPL
content:
Multi-Agent Preference Learning (MAPL) improves collaborating agents by comparing joint responses to the same task. A preference identifies a better and a worse joint response, so each agent learns in the context of the team’s outcome.
CoMLRL provides two approaches: MADPO directly optimizes the policies from preference pairs, while MARLHF first learns a joint reward model and then trains the policies with that reward. Their iterative variants refresh the preference data as training progresses. MAPL names this family of methods; the public trainer classes are MADPOTrainer, MARLHFTrainer, MADPOIterTrainer, and MARLHFIterTrainer.
Explore the three parts of a preference-training setup:
Training Paradigms: Actor and comparator generation modes, joint-response adapters, and iterative training. Comparator: Current policies, model checkpoints, historical policies, and remote APIs. Replay Buffer: Current-round data, recent iterations, full history, and age-weighted sampling. Preference Pairs# For a task with per-agent prompts \( \mathbf{h}=(h_1,\ldots,h_N) \), the trainer samples candidate joint responses \( \mathbf{a}^{k}=(a_1^k,\ldots,a_N^k) \). Candidates with the same index are aligned across agents and receive a shared scalar task reward. A pair is ordered as \( \mathbf{a}^{+}\succ\mathbf{a}^{-} \) when the first response has a strictly higher reward. Ties are discarded.
The training dataset contains task items used to construct prompts. By default, the formatter reads each item’s prompt field; custom formatters can use other fields or provide different prompts for each role. The trainers generate and score their own preference pairs from these items. The base MADPO and MARLHF trainers collect those pairs once before optimization.
All four preference trainers currently require num_turns=1 and aligned joint responses (joint_mode="aligned"). The iterative variants repeat data collection and training; an iteration is not a dialog turn.
MADPO# Multi-Agent Direct Preference Optimization (MADPO) uses a joint preference loss across the agents. Let \( s_{\theta_i}(h_i,a_i) \) denote the completion log-probability score computed by agent \( i \). Its preference margin is:
\[ \Delta_i = s_{\theta_i}(h_i,a_i^{+})-s_{\theta_i}(h_i,a_i^{-}). \] The implemented loss is:
\[ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MADPO}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) =-\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{h},\mathbf{a}^{+},\mathbf{a}^{-})\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pref}}} \left[\log\sigma\!\left(\beta\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta_i\right)\right]. \] Here \( \sigma \) is the sigmoid function and \( \beta \) is dpo_beta. During each agent’s update, the other agents’ margins are detached from the computation graph. The preference signal therefore depends on the joint response, while gradients flow through the agent being updated.
MADPOConfig Parameters num_agents: Number of agents in decentralized mode, or task roles in centralized mode collaboration_mode: "decentralized" (default) or "centralized" num_train_epochs: Number of optimization epochs over the collected preference pairs agent_learning_rate: Learning rate for the policy optimizers preference_num_candidates: Candidates sampled per task and actor; must be at least 2 preference_pairs_per_sample: Maximum selected pairs per task, or None for no limit pair_selection: "reward_gap" selects the largest reward gaps, "random" shuffles valid pairs, and "all" retains every non-tied pair dpo_beta: Positive multiplier on the joint preference margin train_batch_size: Number of preference pairs per update; defaults to rollout_buffer_size max_new_tokens, temperature, top_p, top_k: Candidate generation settings parallel_training, agent_devices: Policy execution mode and device placement eval_interval, eval_num_samples, eval_batch_size: Evaluation schedule and sample sizes logging_steps: Training logging interval MADPOTrainer Parameters agent_model or agents: Model identifier for homogeneous agents, or a list of model identifiers/instances num_agents: Number of agents or task roles; match args.num_agents tokenizer: Tokenizer, or one tokenizer per actor train_dataset: Task items from which preference candidates are generated eval_dataset: Optional evaluation dataset reward_func: Required callable returning one shared reward per aligned joint response reward_processor: Optional post-processing of task rewards formatters: One prompt formatter shared across roles, or a list of role-specific formatters args: MADPOConfig instance model_config: Optional model loading configuration wandb_config: Optional Weights & Biases configuration eval_logger, eval_aggregator: Optional evaluation metrics hooks, as in MAGRPOTrainer centralized_comparator_adapter: Prompt builder and response parser for centralized actors or comparators MADPO currently uses a reference-free preference objective: its loss contains no reference-policy log-probability ratio and does not apply the optional reference KL settings inherited from the shared configuration. Set preference_pairs_per_sample=None when using pair_selection="all". If every candidate reward is tied, the base trainer has no preference pairs to optimize and returns without updates.
The current decentralized scoring helper omits the last completion token after trimming padding; the centralized helper scores the full completion. The formula above uses the score returned by the implementation. This token-boundary difference is an implementation limitation.
MARLHF# Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (MARLHF) separates reward learning from policy learning. In the current implementation, preference labels are obtained from the supplied task reward_func; the public training entry point starts from task items and generates the comparisons.
The JointRewardModel reads the combined prompts and responses of the team. It uses a causal language model backbone and a scalar reward head applied to the final non-padding token. Given a preferred and a rejected response, the reward model minimizes:
\[ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reward}}(\phi) =-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pref}}} \left[\log\sigma\!\left(r_{\phi}(\mathbf{h},\mathbf{a}^{+})-r_{\phi}(\mathbf{h},\mathbf{a}^{-})\right)\right]. \] After reward training, its scores are used without reward-model gradients during online policy optimization. Choose the policy optimizer with rl_algorithm: "magrpo", "mareinforce", "maremax", "marloo", "maac", or "iac". Evaluation continues to use the original task reward, allowing policy performance to be checked independently of the learned reward.
MARLHFConfig Parameters Shared MADPO settings control preference collection, collaboration, generation, and policy training; dpo_beta is not used by the reward-model loss rl_algorithm: Online policy-training algorithm; defaults to "magrpo" num_generations: Online candidates per prompt and actor; at least 2 for the MAGRPO family, or at least 1 for MAAC/IAC reward_model_name: Model identifier for the reward backbone; defaults to the actor model identifier when available reward_model_device: Reward-model device; defaults to "cuda:0", or use None to inherit the trainer device reward_learning_rate, reward_num_train_epochs, reward_train_batch_size: Reward-model optimization settings reward_max_length: Optional token limit for the combined reward-model input reward_freeze_backbone: Train only the scalar reward head when True critic_model_name, critic_learning_rate, critic_devices: Critic settings for an actor-critic backend critic_type: "v" or "q" for an actor-critic backend use_separate_critic: Select separate critics or actor-attached value heads for IAC value_loss_coef, value_clip_range: Critic loss weight and IAC shared-value-head clipping; see Actor-Critic reference_kl_enabled, reference_kl_coef, reference_devices: Optional frozen-reference regularization for the online RL stage MARLHFTrainer Parameters Uses the same task dataset, actor, tokenizer, reward, and formatter inputs as MADPOTrainer, with args=MARLHFConfig(...) critic_model or critics: Optional critic sources for the MAAC/IAC backend. critic_model must be a model identifier string; loaded model instances must be supplied through critics. Use a one-element list for MAAC or one entry per actor for separate-critic IAC. Without explicit sources, critic_model_name or the actor model identifier is used metrics_callback: Optional custom metrics callback for the actor-critic backend Provide reward_model_name when actors are supplied as model objects without a model identifier. Likewise, MAAC or separate-critic IAC needs explicit critic sources or a usable critic model identifier. MARLHF remains single-turn even when the selected RL backend supports multi-turn training on its own.
Iterative Training# MADPOIterTrainer and MARLHFIterTrainer alternate preference collection with optimization. See Training Paradigms for the training cycle and configuration, Comparator for comparison policies, and Replay Buffer for historical data selection.
Collaboration Modes# Preference training supports separate policies per role or one actor generating the complete joint response. See Training Paradigms for the supported actor/comparator layouts and centralized adapters.

title: Replay Buffer
content:
Iterative preference training collects a new set of comparison pairs each round. The replay buffer decides which collected pairs are used for that round’s updates. It is shared by MADPOIterTrainer and MARLHFIterTrainer.
The current round is written before replay selection, so it is eligible alongside earlier rounds. Replay controls the training data; the comparator policy controls how new candidate responses are generated.
Replay Modes# Mode Eligible preference data current All pairs from the current round, without historical sampling. nearest_k The latest preference_replay_k non-empty iteration datasets, including the current one when non-empty. all_history Every recorded non-empty iteration dataset in the current trainer run. lambda_decay The same history, with greater sampling weight on more recent datasets when λ is below 1. nearest_k means recent iterations in time. It does not perform nearest-neighbor retrieval by embedding or similarity.
all_history makes all recorded iterations eligible; it does not necessarily train on every historical pair in each round. For nearest_k and all_history, eligible iteration datasets have equal selection weight, regardless of how many pairs each contains.
Lambda Decay# preference_replay_lambda controls how quickly the probability of selecting an older dataset decreases. If age 0 denotes the newest non-empty dataset and there are \( K \) eligible datasets, the normalized weight for age \( a \) is:
\[ w_a = \frac{(1-\lambda)\lambda^a}{\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}(1-\lambda)\lambda^j}, \qquad 0 \leq \lambda < 1. \] lambda=0 selects only the newest non-empty dataset. Values between 0 and 1 assign progressively less weight to older datasets. lambda=1 is handled separately and gives every eligible dataset equal weight. The weights apply to iteration datasets, then pairs are sampled within each selected dataset. A smaller λ emphasizes recent experience while a larger λ keeps more earlier data in the sampling distribution.
Sampling Size# Historical replay first samples dataset assignments, then samples pairs from each selected dataset. Within one dataset, sampling uses no repeated pairs when its assigned count fits in that dataset. Larger assigned counts cycle through shuffled copies of the dataset, so repeated pairs are possible. The combined sample is shuffled before training.
By default, preference_replay_sample_size uses the number of pairs collected in the current round. If that round has no pairs, it uses the size of the latest non-empty dataset. An explicit positive sample size overrides this behavior.
Replay Buffer parameters:
preference_replay_mode: "current" (default), "nearest_k", "all_history", or "lambda_decay" preference_replay_k: Positive number of recent non-empty datasets eligible for "nearest_k"; required in that mode preference_replay_lambda: Age-decay parameter in [0, 1]; required only for "lambda_decay" preference_replay_sample_size: Positive number of pairs sampled for historical replay, or None for the default described above preference_replay_dir: Optional location for serialized preference datasets current rejects preference_replay_sample_size and preference_replay_lambda; its preference_replay_k may be None or 1. For the historical modes, use preference_replay_k only with nearest_k and preference_replay_lambda only with lambda_decay.
Configuration Examples# Recent iterations:
from comlrl.trainers.preference import MADPOIterConfig args = MADPOIterConfig( num_agents=2, preference_replay_mode="nearest_k", preference_replay_k=3, preference_replay_sample_size=256, )Age-weighted history:
from comlrl.trainers.preference import MADPOIterConfig args = MADPOIterConfig( num_agents=2, preference_replay_mode="lambda_decay", preference_replay_lambda=0.8, preference_replay_sample_size=256, )The same replay options are available in MARLHFIterConfig. Both examples configure sampling only; model sources, datasets, reward functions, and the other trainer inputs are supplied separately.
Saved Preference Data# The trainer writes each round to iteration_0001.json, iteration_0002.json, and so on under the replay directory. Records contain the prompts, preferred and rejected completions, rewards, and associated preference metadata. Historical samples are reconstructed from this text using the actor tokenizers.
The in-memory replay index tracks datasets produced by the current trainer instance. Setting preference_replay_dir changes the output location; it does not automatically import an earlier run’s files.
Actor checkpoints are stored separately through policy_checkpoint_dir. They provide model weights for a history comparator, while the replay buffer stores preference examples used for training.

title: Logging Metric
content:
Save evaluation results locally, record training curves in Weights & Biases, and add task-specific metrics. The examples below build on the trainer and held-out split in Dataset Loading.
Local Metrics# Evaluation returns a metrics dictionary even when W&B is disabled. Save it locally if you only need a record of a completed evaluation:
import json from pathlib import Path # Use the MAGRPO trainer and eval_dataset from the Dataset Loading guide. metrics = trainer.evaluate(num_eval_samples=len(eval_dataset)) Path("eval-metrics.json").write_text(json.dumps(metrics, indent=2) + "\n")Weights & Biases# To record training curves in Weights & Biases, pass wandb_config when constructing the trainer:
wandb_config = { "project": "comlrl", "name": "length-ratio-magrpo", "tags": ["length-ratio", "magrpo"], "config_sections": { "dataset": {"name": "length-ratio", "split_seed": 42}, "output": {"verbose": True}, }, } # Add this keyword when constructing MAGRPOTrainer: # wandb_config=wandb_config,Authenticate W&B in your environment before enabling it. Omit wandb_config or set it to None to disable W&B. The supported run settings include project, entity, name (or run_name), tags, and dir; config_sections adds your dataset and experiment settings to the recorded configuration. config_sections.output.verbose controls trainer progress output.
Training Metrics# For the MARL trainers, logs use env_step, which counts joint-action reward evaluations. It is different from a dataset index or optimizer-update count, especially with multiple generations or turns. logging_steps sets the minimum gap in this counter between standard training metric logs, emitted when rollout buffers are processed. Evaluation follows eval_interval independently.
Metric Meaning turn_1/reward_mean Mean immediate reward in the logged training rollouts at turn 1 turn_1/expected_return Mean return stored for those training rollouts eval/turn_1/reward_mean Mean immediate reward in evaluation rollouts at turn 1 eval/turn_1/expected_return Mean evaluation return from turn 1 Turn numbers start at 1. MAGRPO evaluation returns are undiscounted sums of rewards from the current turn onward; IAC and MAAC report their collected rollout returns. Rewards reflect the configured reward processing, and actor-critic returns can also include reference-KL shaping when enabled. The single-turn example in Dataset Loading uses the default identity reward processor and no reference KL, so its reward and return metrics describe the same task score.
Custom Metrics# MAGRPO accepts an eval_logger and an eval_aggregator together. The logger receives completions in [agent][dataset item][turn] order plus the original batch_items and raw prompts. The aggregator returns scalar metrics without the eval/ prefix; the trainer adds it.
For example, measure the average response length across agents at each turn:
def eval_logger(*, agent_completions_turns, batch_items, prompts): return [ { f"turn_{turn + 1}/response_chars": sum( len(agent[row][turn]) for agent in agent_completions_turns ) / len(agent_completions_turns) for turn in range(len(agent_completions_turns[0][row])) } for row in range(len(batch_items)) ] def eval_aggregator(rows, *, num_turns): return { key: sum(row[key] for row in rows) / len(rows) for turn in range(num_turns) for key in [f"turn_{turn + 1}/response_chars"] } if rows else {} # Add both keywords when constructing MAGRPOTrainer: # eval_logger=eval_logger, # eval_aggregator=eval_aggregator,The resulting dictionary includes eval/turn_1/response_chars. These callbacks also receive metadata fields, so you can compute task-specific accuracy or group metrics without placing reference answers in the prompts.
IAC and MAAC instead accept metrics_callback(rollouts), which returns a dictionary of numeric values. Each rollout sample provides fields such as agent_idx, prompt, completion, and metadata:
def metrics_callback(rollouts): if not rollouts: return {} return { "response_chars": sum(len(sample.completion) for sample in rollouts) / len(rollouts) } # Add metrics_callback=metrics_callback to IACTrainer(...) or MAACTrainer(...).This callback runs during both training and evaluation. Evaluation averages its values across evaluated dataset items and adds eval/; training logs its values at rollout collection time, separately from the standard logging_steps gate.
